integrity_statement: This is an append-only delta checkpoint. The twenty admissions, eighty observations, and sixteen universal families in v0.3 remain controlling. Five independent challenge sources were reviewed from complete publisher text, final open-access article text, or complete author or institutional manuscripts reconciled to the published DOI. They contribute twenty atomic observations and one new universal family. Abstract-only records, search snippets, press summaries, and unqualified working papers do not count. Academic quantities remain prompt-time reasoning examples and never become current platform facts.

challenge_design.question: Does an independent set of evidence on cross-country employment, wage incidence, firm payoff thresholds, complementary intangible investment, establishment-to-aggregate transmission, and AI-stack market power add more than two universal reasoning families or reopen a foundation gap?
attack_surface: employment effects may reverse across countries, skill groups, and levels of aggregation
employment growth in exposed occupations may fail to reach wages
low-intensity adoption may produce no detectable firm payoff
unmeasured intangible investment may distort the timing of aggregate productivity
firm gains and consumer benefits may accrue as concentrated rents rather than broad welfare
independence_controls: five sources not admitted in the foundation or first challenge
cross-country occupation, venture survey, national growth-accounting, establishment vacancy, and industrial-organization designs represented
employment, wages, revenue, measured productivity, skill demand, consumer surplus, and market power kept separate
positive, negative, delayed, and statistically undetectable outcomes represented
no academic quantity is authorized as a live platform observation

verified_admissions_delta.title: New Technologies and Jobs in Europe

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 59-page Banco de España institutional manuscript and November 2024 author draft reconciled to the Economic Policy publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: occupation-level potential exposure to AI and software -> changes in sector-occupation employment shares and relative wages -> variation by worker composition and national institutions
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Three-digit occupations in sector-occupation cells across fifteen euro-area countries and the United Kingdom from 2011 through 2019, using EU-LFS employment and wage measures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Employment shares rise on average in more AI-exposed occupations, especially those with younger and more-skilled workers; wage evidence is weak, and national results vary with diffusion, education, product-market regulation, and employment protection
limitations: Exposure indices do not observe firm adoption or generative-AI use
The estimates are associations at occupation-sector level rather than randomized causal effects
Employment-share changes need not equal changes in employment levels
The 2011-2019 period predates mass-market generative AI
Cross-country correlates are suggestive and may reflect omitted institutional differences

anti_patterns: Do not treat potential exposure as observed adoption.
Do not relabel an employment-share change as net job creation.
Do not infer wage gains from employment-share gains.
Do not erase country, skill, or age heterogeneity behind the pooled coefficient.

verified_admissions_delta.title: Concentrating Intelligence: Scaling and Market Structure in Artificial Intelligence

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 32-page INET author manuscript reconciled to the Economic Policy publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: high fixed training and adaptation costs plus low operating costs, scarce inputs, and scope economies -> provider competition, entry barriers, tipping, and vertical integration -> market power and distribution of AI value
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Industrial-organization analysis of the foundation-model stack using market, cost, input, investment, and capability evidence available through September 2024
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Fierce model-level competition can coexist with concentrated compute and cloud inputs; open-source distribution, capability convergence, breakthroughs, demand scale, and vertical ties can change contestability
limitations: The market snapshot ages quickly in a rapidly changing industry
Several cost, share, and investment observations rely on external estimates rather than audited public accounts
Natural-monopoly tendencies are mechanisms and scenarios, not proof of a durable monopoly
Transformative-AI implications are explicitly speculative
Policy effects are analyzed rather than empirically identified

anti_patterns: Do not equate high fixed costs with observed monopoly.
Do not infer broad welfare from provider revenue or valuation.
Do not treat current market share as durable when capabilities, prices, and open-source alternatives are moving.
Do not ignore upstream compute and cloud concentration when describing model competition.

verified_admissions_delta.title: When Does AI Pay Off? AI-Adoption Intensity, Complementary Investments, and R&D Strategy

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 15-page published article PDF and author manuscript

verified_extraction.claim_path: surveyed NLP, computer-vision, or machine-learning adoption intensity -> firm revenue growth -> moderation by database, cloud, and firm-specific R&D investment
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: High-tech ventures in South Korea surveyed in 2019 and linked to administrative and retrospectively reported firm characteristics; the main growth sample is a selected subset of surviving firms
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Low adoption intensity is not significantly related to revenue growth; positive associations appear at higher intensity and chiefly among ventures with complementary data, cloud, and internal R&D capabilities
limitations: The observational design cannot eliminate omitted-variable or reverse-causality bias
Adoption intensity is self-reported in broad categories
The analysis assumes little or no AI adoption at the retrospective base year
Revenue growth is not productivity, profit, wages, or welfare
High-tech South Korean ventures are not representative of all firms or countries

anti_patterns: Do not treat testing or low-intensity use as evidence of realized firm payoff.
Do not infer causality from the revenue-growth association.
Do not generalize a high-tech venture threshold mechanically to large incumbents or other countries.
Do not omit the complementary data, cloud, and R&D conditions.

verified_admissions_delta.title: The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 55-page NBER author manuscript reconciled to the AEA publication and replication record

verified_extraction.claim_path: new general-purpose technology -> complementary intangible investment and foregone current output -> later capital services -> difference between true and measured productivity across the adoption cycle
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Formal growth-accounting model applied to U.S. computer-hardware and software capital using national accounts and estimated intangible complements through 2017
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Measured productivity can understate true productivity during intangible-capital formation and overstate it when previously accumulated complements yield services; timing and magnitude depend on investment and depreciation assumptions
limitations: Empirical calibration uses earlier computer hardware and software rather than realized generative-AI investment
Many organization, training, data, and process intangibles are unobserved and modeled
The J-curve is a measurement mechanism, not a guarantee of eventual payoff
National-account treatment differs from firm accounting and from welfare measurement
Results depend on capital-service, depreciation, and counterfactual assumptions

anti_patterns: Do not use the J-curve to excuse every weak productivity result.
Do not call all current spending productive intangible capital.
Do not infer future gains unless complementary assets are actually accumulated and produce services.
Do not confuse measured TFP, true productivity, output, and welfare.

verified_admissions_delta.title: Artificial Intelligence and Jobs: Evidence from Online Vacancies

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 49-page MIT open-access final published version

verified_extraction.claim_path: establishment task suitability -> posting of AI vacancies as an adoption proxy -> changes in non-AI hiring and requested skills -> tests for aggregate occupation and industry employment and wages
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Near-universe of U.S. online vacancies from 2010 through 2018 linked at establishment, firm, occupation, industry, commuting-zone, and skill levels
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: AI-adopting exposed establishments reduce non-AI vacancy posting and alter requested skills, yet aggregate employment and wage effects in exposed occupations and industries remain too small to detect in the sample period
limitations: Vacancies measure intended hiring rather than filled jobs, incumbent employment, or task execution
AI vacancies are a narrow adoption proxy and miss systems deployed without AI hiring
The study predates mass-market generative AI
Establishment effects can be offset by reallocation, entry, demand, and spillovers elsewhere
Statistically undetectable aggregate effects are not proof of zero effect

anti_patterns: Do not promote an establishment hiring response into an aggregate employment claim.
Do not treat absence of a detectable aggregate coefficient as proof of no effect.
Do not equate AI vacancies with installed AI or use intensity.
Do not equate requested skills, vacancies, hires, employment, and wages.

verified_atomic_observations_delta.statement: The relationship between AI exposure and employment varies across countries, worker skill, age composition, and institutional regimes.
Employment-share gains in exposed occupations need not be accompanied by relative-wage gains.
Occupation exposure can organize heterogeneous labor evidence but cannot identify actual firm adoption.
Country-level diffusion, education, competition, and employment-protection correlations remain suggestive rather than isolated causal mechanisms.
High fixed costs, low operating costs, and economies of scope can concentrate provider value even when model capabilities are widely useful.
Fierce foundation-model competition can coexist with concentrated upstream compute, cloud, data, or talent inputs.
Open-source distribution can expand consumer surplus and downstream innovation without generating equivalent provider revenue.
Market structure is regime-dependent because capability convergence, breakthroughs, prices, demand, vertical ties, and entry can move rapidly.
Any adoption and adoption intensity can yield different conclusions about firm performance.
Data systems, cloud infrastructure, and firm-specific R&D can condition whether adoption translates into revenue growth.
Testing and low-intensity use may precede detectable payoff while firms accumulate complements and redesign processes.
An observational revenue-growth threshold is evidence of conditional association, not a universal causal adoption threshold.
Organizational change, training, data, process redesign, and other intangibles are productive complements rather than free add-ons to a general-purpose technology.
Measured productivity can lag during complementary investment and rise later when accumulated intangible capital yields services.
A productivity J-curve is a conditional measurement mechanism, not proof that every technology investment will pay off.
Measured TFP, true productivity, output, revenue, profit, and welfare remain distinct outcomes across the investment cycle.
AI-vacancy posting is a narrow establishment-adoption proxy rather than direct observation of installed systems or workflow use.
An adopting establishment can reduce non-AI vacancy demand while changing the skill mix of the positions it continues to post.
A visible establishment response can remain too small to detect after aggregation to occupations or industries.
A statistically undetectable aggregate effect is not proof of a precisely zero economic effect.

new_universal_families.label: market structure, rents, consumer surplus, and value incidence
new_universal_families.rule: Separate productive value created from revenue, profit, valuation, consumer surplus, worker compensation, input rents, and market power; trace where value accrues across model, compute, cloud, data, application, firm, worker, and consumer layers, conditional on entry barriers, scale and scope economies, openness, vertical integration, and the competitive regime.

saturation_assessment.reason: The second independent batch deepened scale alignment, exposure discipline, adoption intensity, complementary capital, diffusion lags, employment and wage separation, statistical-null interpretation, and firm-to-aggregate transmission. Only the distribution of value across competition, rents, consumer surplus, workers, and stack inputs required a new family. The challenge remains below the two-family saturation ceiling and reopens no foundation gap.

next_action: Run a five-source integrated confirmation across human-AI teamwork, workflow role allocation, strategic decision-making, adoption behavior, and economy-wide transmission. Confirm that the seventeen-family architecture explains the evidence without adding a new universal family, then complete the two-text long-form passage audit.
